item.title: A look at OpenAI’s math that’s claimed computes faster Fourier transforms (121 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.argmin.net/p/faster-fourier-transforms, See on Hacker News

Hi there, argmin readers! Today’s post looks at part of OpenAI’s math repository that claims to compute faster Fourier transforms. It’s more technical than usual, but I tried to add some tutorial material for people who need a refresher course on signal processing or computational complexity.

The Fast Fourier Transform is one of the most important innovations in digital signal processing and one of my favorite algorithms. The FFT is a fast way to extract the frequency content of signals, letting you rapidly analyze, filter, and manipulate frequencies across different bands of the spectrum.

The Fourier transform computes the energy in each frequency band through a simple dot product.1 Let x denote your input, a length n array of samples, and f a frequency. Then the amount of frequency content in x at f can be computed by the formula:

For digital signals, a bit of math shows you only need to compute n of these dot products, one at each multiple of the frequency 2𝜋/n, to understand all of the frequency content. Naively, this requires n multiplications and additions for each frequency. Hence, computing the entire Fourier transform appears to require n2 arithmetic operations.

The fast Fourier transform is a clever recursive procedure devised by James Cooley and John Tukey in 1965.2 The main idea is that a length-n Fourier transform can be computed by shuffling the input vector, computing two Fourier transforms of length n/2 on the shuffled components, and then recombining the outputs using atomic arithmetic operations. The shuffles and recombinations take a linear number of arithmetic operations. Repeating this procedure iteratively, namely, log2(n) times, computes the full discrete Fourier transform. With the bookkeeping, the FFT computes a length-n Fourier transform in fewer than 5 n log2 n arithmetic operations.

To make this acceleration concrete, when n is 1,000, n^2 is 1,000,000 and 5 * n log n is around 50,000, a 20-fold speedup. When n is 1,000,000, the speedup is 10,000-fold. These speedups can be the difference between a transform being computable or not given the constraints of a signal processing application.

Since the invention of the FFT, people have looked for even faster Fourier transforms. One question is just how fast you can go. It seems like you probably need at least n operations to compute the FFT, as it takes n steps just to write it down. The FFT is 5*log2(n) times slower than that reasonable speed limit, and that 5*log2(n) factor can be big. It’s 200 when n is a trillion. Can you do something clever to reduce that prefactor of 200?

Well, lo and behold, in the massive paper dump OpenAI took on the mathematics world last week, they claim to have a faster Fourier transform. The main claim from their discriminatively named “main.pdf” is

I was intrigued about what was going on here. The log(n) term, in theory, was a teeny tiny bit smaller than in the standard FFT.

Did I read this paper? Of course not. No one at OpenAI read this paper either, so why should I? I did what every other mathematician in the world does with AI slop mathematics: I fed it back into the slop machine and ran an information retrieval session with a chatbot interface to extract salient facts. Anthropomorphically speaking: I asked ChatGPT what it thinks about its own output. This is how we do mathematical research now. What a world.

Unfortunately, I did not find a faster Fourier transform. Instead,l I found the rot that develops inside applied mathematical theory when formalism becomes so detached from reality that a “breakthrough” is nothing more than an artifact of mathematicians not being able to properly specify the rules of their games in natural language.

First, “big-O” notation has been so abused that it has become meaningless. Let’s review the definition, which impressed me as an undergrad. An algorithm has running time T(n) = O(F(n)) if there exists an integer N and a constant C such that

That is, the number of steps the algorithm actually takes is upper bounded by a constant times some convenient function F(n) as long as n is large. F(n) is usually something familiar and interpretable, like a polynomial or exponential function. This notation says that we only care about what happens when the size of the computation is large. We care about the asymptotic growth rate of the computation time. All constants are equivalent.

Big-O notation is useful for shortcuts in algorithmic accounting, but it also allows for remarkable logical laziness. If we want a practically faster FFT, we want an algorithm that requires fewer than 50n operations for reasonably sized n. But O(n) does not mean 50 n. It could mean 1080 n. This would be considered a “linear time” algorithm. An algorithm that requires n + 1080 is also considered a linear time algorithm in the big-O regime. An algorithm that only has linear-time guarantees when n is greater than 1080 is also considered linear time. 1080 is approximately equal to the number of atoms in the known universe. That is why Richard Lipton and Ken Regan call algorithms with unfathomably large hidden constants galactic algorithms.

The OpenAI FFT algorithm is definitely galactic. The estimated values for C were 10100 when N=1012. So even when n=10100, the venerable Cooley-Tukey-Gauss FFT would be 1099 times faster.

So why is this new FFT result interesting? Well, note that in big-O notation, it is technically asymptotically faster than the Cooley-Tukey algorithm because

I mean, sure. But given the constants, the algorithm runs faster only when n is impossibly large. Roughly, you need

whatever the hell that number means.

Lipton and Regan argue galactic algorithms are useful because they spur research. Once you show a running time is asymptotically possible, you can spend your time finding an algorithm that practically achieves this provable running time. Maybe you can send your AI agent swarms after it. You do you. Maybe you can get a practical algorithm out, but I don’t know of any legitimate examples where this happened. I’m particularly doubtful here, because the model of “computation” OpenAI uses bears no resemblance to an actual computer.

“The model uses exact complex arithmetic.” That means it assumes you can store and multiply complex numbers at arbitrary precision. Indeed, the algorithm requires you to multiply complex numbers whose magnitudes grow superpolynomially with n. If you stored these numbers as bits, the memory requirement would effectively be exponential in the input length. It assumes you can multiply such arbitrarily large complex numbers together in a single operation. We do not have computers that can do this. So even if this theorem in main.pdf is “true” (no one knows, and I don’t care), it’s not actually solving the problem we set out to solve when looking for a faster FFT.

For people familiar with theoretical analyses of the FFT, that you need an absurd model of computation to break the FFT speed limit isn’t surprising. In 1973, Jacques Morgenstern proved that you couldn’t get a Fourier transform faster than ½ n log n if you required that complex coefficients used in the computation had bounded magnitude. That should have been the end of the story! But it wasn’t. People said Morgenstern’s restricted coefficient model was too restrictive. Forty years later, Nir Ailon showed that you couldn’t compute an FFT faster than n log n without severe numerical instabilities. This was also too restrictive for some people, I guess.

This new OpenAI result is thus less a mathematical breakthrough and more an oddity of computer scientists being bad at formalizing their design specifications. The “theoretical” definition of a computer is very far removed from the computers we actually build. The “faster” Fourier transform is merely an example where theory gets so unmoored from the original question that an “open problem” becomes nothing more than an academic status puzzle. The solution is like what happens when you set computational bot streams at impossible problems and find them engaging in illegal hacking.

Many of the other “big” results in this OpenAI slopository could be critiqued in the same way. For example, one of those results was a galactic algorithm to multiply two matrices in O(n^2.25) operations. The construction used in the paper does not let you even estimate the constant that hides inside big O.3 It may as well be infinite, computable only with the divine music of the spheres.

Still, if written substantially better, these papers would have made it into the most prestigious publication venues for the theory of computer science (i.e., refereed conference proceedings from STOC or FOCS).4 The matrix multiplication paper would have likely won awards. But neither of these has anything to do with computers!

This is because the theory of computer science has a culture that actively discourages running algorithms on a computer. It’s acceptable to write papers in theory conferences that assert an algorithm exists without ever writing it down. The theory of computer science has become a form of mathematics that doesn’t concern itself with computers, and it offers little reward for impact outside those mathematical pursuits. I explained this to a friend who remarked to me that “theory” has the transdisciplinary meaning of “hiding in obscurity of one’s own making.”

AI is really good at automating our worst tendencies. It amplifies the unspoken cultural practices no one likes, but no individual can reasonably deviate from. It exploits the mechanized traditions recalcitrant to collective action. In that vein, AI can now write useless theory papers. But perhaps in the absurdity of the distasteful OpenAI trash dump of proofs, we can all look up and realize together that we should consider doing something else.

item.title: Leaving Tech (151 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://ryanbigg.com/2026/10/leaving-tech, See on Hacker News

I’ve now applied for over 3 dozen jobs and I’ve heard back from 24 of them with a rejection. This tech market at the moment is so very cooked and for that reason I’m stepping away from tech.

I’ve been a developer for 20 years across more than just the Ruby and JavaScript that I’m known for. I’ve written books about programming, I’ve given talks and I’ve ran events. I maintain two of the most downloaded Ruby packages. And yes, I delivered the fuck out of value for shareholders. I also grew a team from 2 people to 12 people at my last job.

I cannot continue to put myself through this process of rejection. It is causing me a great deal of mental harm and anguish.

The industry at the moment wants people who know how to use AI to further the business goals but here’s the thing nobody wants to admit: not one person knows how to use AI to actually do that. I use it to write a lot of my code and then I critically review that code before it reaches production.

My life is based here in Warrnambool and I choose to work remotely from here. Hybrid is infeasible even if it were in Melbourne because Melbourne is 3.5hrs away on the train. I know I can work remotely effectively because I did it for the last 6 years. And I helped others adjust to that as well!

So it’s clear that there’s no room for me in tech anymore, so I’m going to chat to some people to figure out what’s next.

item.title: AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities (192 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13928, See on Hacker News

View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract:Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training on a small chemical reaction prediction task - a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. We release our models to support the improvement of defenses.

item.title: I turned my unused Kindle into a photo frame with GPT-6 Astra (143 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://nirajrajgor.com/blog/kindle-photo-frame-with-ai, See on Hacker News

My Kindle was sitting unused, so I decided to see whether AI could help me find a new use for it. I wanted to create a custom app that could cover a range of uses and be controlled by an AI agent on my MacBook.

I started with a small goal: use my own image as the Kindle's screensaver. Once that worked, I asked the agent to build an app that could cycle through a collection of photos.

We called the project KindleCTL. On my Kindle, I open "Photo Slideshow" from the same screen where I choose my books. It cycles through ten photos, showing each for four minutes. When I want to read, I exit the slideshow and return to my books.

I used Codex and T3 Code on my Mac to work with the coding agents.

I first tried GPT-5.6 Sol with reasoning effort set to Extra High. It wrote code to connect to the Kindle but couldn't resolve an error that prevented it from storing data on the device. Then I tried Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, but Anthropic's cybersecurity safeguards blocked each attempt after two prompts. Finally, I tried GPT-6 Astra with reasoning effort set to High. We were able to jailbreak the Kindle.

We used the existing jailbreak code as a reference to build our own tools for running custom software on the Kindle. Then we created and installed the slideshow app.

The slideshow passed its automated checks on my Mac, but switching photos on the Kindle left traces of the previous image on screen. The tests hadn't caught how the physical display refreshed. Getting from passing tests to something I could use turned out to be the most interesting part of the experiment.

Let's walk through how we went from an unused Kindle to a working photo frame, starting with getting the agent connected.

Connecting the agent to the Kindle

I started in an empty project folder with a 10th-generation Kindle Basic. I gave the agent its network address and device details. We had no USB connection, so the entire setup happened over Wi-Fi.

From there, we still needed to set up access to run our own software on the Kindle.

The GPT-5.6 Sol attempt got as far as loading a helper on the Kindle, but the program that helper was meant to start never reported that it was ready to execute. It couldn't locate a filesystem where it could store content.

The attempts with Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 were both blocked by Anthropic's cybersecurity safeguards after two prompts. Then I tried GPT-6 Astra. I explicitly asked it to build the custom software we needed for personal use and take inspiration from existing open-source projects.

We adapted the existing jailbreak from SpiderCat, released by sparklerfish and the KindleModding community, and built custom tools called KindleCTL around it.

  • What we built: Tools to send commands from my Mac, transfer files, and investigate errors on the Kindle.
  • What broke: Our launcher crashed before it could start. We traced that to a compatibility issue with the Kindle's older system software and fixed how the launcher was built.
  • How we checked: We connected with administrator access, transferred files both ways, and displayed text. Later, we verified that access still worked after a reboot.

The feedback loop was the game changer

Initially, the agent could connect to the Kindle but couldn't display data. To debug this, it asked me for pictures of the Kindle's screen. I took photos with my phone and shared them with the agent on my Mac.

This was becoming tedious. Since the agent was connected to the Kindle, I wondered why it couldn't get this information itself. I asked it to set up a feedback loop so it could access logs without me having to share screenshots.

The agent set up a persistent diagnostic connection so it could collect errors and test fixes without asking me to download and reopen a package each time. Later, we added remote screen captures so it could also inspect what the Kindle was displaying.

This was a turning point that let the agent continue implementing changes on autopilot. Its reasoning traces showed it figuring out which folders survived a restart and which could store external data.

I was surprised the agent hadn't suggested this on its own. Once I asked for a feedback loop, it set one up and could test fixes without my help.

Most of the code was written in Python. The Kindle's launcher and slideshow were written in C, with shell scripts handling installation and device controls.

With the connection working, I asked the agent to try a small test first: transfer an image and set it as the Kindle's screensaver. I checked that the image appeared correctly and that waking the Kindle brought back the normal Home screen. Once that worked, I asked for the slideshow app.

Getting the slideshow working

I asked the agent for a looping slideshow of ten photos, with an Exit button. Each photo would fit the screen while keeping its original aspect ratio.

The slides were changing, but the transitions weren't smooth, so I asked the agent to look into it. With the feedback loop already in place, it investigated the issue and used the Kindle's built-in screen refresh mechanism to clear the previous image after each slide change.

The screen captures showed complete images, but they couldn't reveal traces left on the physical display. After the refresh change, I checked the Kindle and confirmed that each photo looked clean.

I customized how long each photo stays on screen and the brightness level. If the Kindle goes to sleep, the slideshow picks up where it left off when it wakes.

For now, I use my Mac to change the photos and slideshow timing. The photos stay stored on the Kindle, so the slideshow works without Wi-Fi. In the future, we could add controls to change the slideshow timing on the Kindle and send photos directly from a phone or another device.

What I learned

Next time, I'd set up the feedback loop from the start so the agent could read logs, inspect screen captures, and test fixes on the device.

The Kindle now sits on our wooden shelf, where we use it every day as a photo frame.

I started because I was curious about what AI could help me do with an unused device. Now I have an app for my photos that works the way I asked, plus the tools to keep experimenting with the Kindle.

Disclaimer: This was a personal experiment on my own Kindle, not a step-by-step jailbreak guide. Only experiment with devices you own or have explicit permission to modify.

One exception: the 3-bit Qwen3-30B reads a prompt slower than llama.cpp, since its Q3_K weights do not go to the GPU's fast prompt yet; it writes three times as fast.

How they were measured, and the speeds with the drafts: What works now. On another machine the figures will be other ones: janas-bench measures yours.

Try it on Linux x86-64 (Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12 and later):

curl -LO https://github.com/prabanta-dev/janas/releases/latest/download/janas-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
tar xf janas-linux-x86_64.tar.gz && cd janas
./janas-chat                     # the models it knows: pick one, it is downloaded and checked

Or on Windows 10 (1903 or later) and 11, x86-64: download janas-windows-x86_64.zip, unpack it, and in a terminal in its janas folder run .\janas-chat. On the same laptop under Windows 11 (12 October 2026) Janas-LLM wrote as fast as on Linux (Qwen3-4B 25.6 tok/s, Qwen3-30B-A3B 34.2) and read a prompt as fast with the mixture (Qwen3-30B-A3B 132 tok/s) and 1.8 times as fast with the dense model (Qwen3-4B 346 tok/s against 193), whose whole blocks go to the GPU, through Intel's own Windows driver there.

The models come already converted from Hugging Face; building from the sources: Getting started.

  ▄███████████▄    
▄███████████████▄  
███ ▄ █████ ▄ ███ ▄   J A N A S
███▄▄▄█████▄▄▄████ 
▀█████▄▀▀▀▄█████▀ ▀   a family of tools for artificial intelligence, in C
  █████████████    
 █ █ █ █ █ █ █ █   
▀ ▀ ▀ ▀ ▀ ▀ ▀ ▀

Janas is a family of tools for artificial intelligence, written in C with no dependencies beyond the C library. Its first component, Janas-LLM, runs large mixture-of-experts language models on ordinary computers, with or without a GPU: the weights stay on disk, the experts each token needs are streamed from an NVMe SSD, and the ones that keep coming back stay in memory. An 80-billion parameter model runs, and answers, on a laptop with 32 GB of RAM.

Designed and written by Maurizio "camauri" Cammalleri.

⚠️ Read this first

This is an experiment, not a product.
Stage Early development. The public API and the command line change without notice, and have changed several times a week. The models' files are the exception: the .jns files published on Hugging Face (format version 2) will be read by every later version of Janas-LLM.
Stability Not verified. The engine is deliberately hard on the machine: it fills the free memory with its expert cache and reads the disk at full speed with O_DIRECT. On a machine with less headroom than it reckons, the desktop can be pushed into swap and become slow or unresponsive. Using a GPU has, once, caused a driver reset that took the desktop with it.
Data It writes only in ~/.cache/janas (what it learns about your machine, and the system messages it has read, so as not to read them again) and where you tell it to put a converted model. It does not touch the model files it reads.
Hardware Developed and run on one machine (below). On anything else it is untested: it may be slower, it may refuse the model, it may misbehave.

If something goes wrong, Ctrl-C stops a reply and Ctrl-D leaves the chat; --cache <GiB> puts a hard limit on the memory it takes, and JANAS_GPU=0 keeps it off the GPU entirely.

The machine it grew on

Everything in this repository was written and measured on:

  • Linux Debian 13 (trixie), x86-64, kernel 6.12.107; GPU driver Mesa 26.1.6 (Vulkan); built with GCC 14.2
  • Intel Core Ultra 9 185H (6 performance cores, 8 efficiency, 2 low-power; AVX2, FMA, F16C, AVX-VNNI; integrated Arc GPU)
  • 32 GB of DDR5 RAM
  • 1 TB NVMe SSD (about 5.7 GB/s reading)

The Windows build was run on the same laptop under Windows 11 (build 26300), with Intel's own graphics driver: its tests pass there, and how fast it was is under Or on Windows, above.

Everything the engine does is chosen from what it measures, so another machine will make other choices — that part is meant to travel. What has never been tried is the rest: other CPUs (especially without AVX-VNNI, or AMD), discrete GPUs, slower disks, more or less memory. If you run it somewhere else, the report from janas-bench is the single most useful thing you can send back (see Helping it run on more hardware).

What works now

What Janas-LLM runs today, model by model and feature by feature: docs/features.md.

On the machine above, with nothing else running, janas-bench reports this (measured on 10 October 2026, with the fast prompt the engine uses by default since that day):

Model reading a prompt writing a reply with drafts, in a chat
Qwen3.5-2B (dense, 1.3 GB) 395 tok/s 50 tok/s 67 tok/s
Qwen3-4B (dense, 2.5 GB) 220 tok/s 28 tok/s see --draft below
Qwen3.5-9B (dense, 5.7 GB) 103 tok/s 14 tok/s 24 tok/s
Qwen3-30B-A3B (18.6 GB) 133 tok/s 34 tok/s —
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (22.3 GB) 86 tok/s 25 tok/s 34 tok/s
Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B (48.4 GB) 64 tok/s 22 tok/s 37 tok/s
Gemma-4-E2B-it (3.1 GB) 211 tok/s 38 tok/s 52 tok/s
Gemma-4-E4B-it (5.0 GB) 133 tok/s 20 tok/s 32 tok/s
Gemma-4-12B-it (dense, 7.1 GB) 71 tok/s 10 tok/s 14 tok/s
Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it (18.3 GB) 90 tok/s 18 tok/s 26 tok/s

Every figure is the mean of three rounds, not a best round, of the configuration the engine itself chose for each kind of pass - the one a chat runs: a prompt of 256 tokens, then 64 written. Here the integrated GPU reads every prompt (the fast prompt, below), and the threads the engine settled on were the performance cores' 12 for a prompt and for a single token on nearly every model, all the usable cores (performance and efficiency, not the low-power ones) for a few tokens at once. On another machine the engine may settle on other threads: the first passes of each kind try every core, one thread per performance core and the performance cores' threads, keep the fastest, and later try the others now and then, so that a machine that warms up can change the verdict (on an i9-14900HX every thread replied at less than half the speed of the performance cores' 16). The rounds run in alternating order so that the machine warming up and the cache filling weigh on each setting alike. Expect a few per cent either way between runs, and rather less than these on a first run, while the cache is still filling. Without the GPU (JANAS_GPU=0) Qwen3-4B reads the same prompt at 85 tok/s and writes at 27.

The last column is a draft guessing the next tokens and the model checking them, which is the same text at a higher rate — the whole of it is explained under --mtp: the Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6 models' and Qwen3-Next's own prediction block, Gemma 4's assistant (a small drafting model of its own). It is measured on a chat reply: an ordinary question in English ("explain how bread is made at home"), 64 tokens of the answer, sampled as the chat samples. What the draft is worth depends on the text: there the drafts survived 74-89% of the time on the Qwen models and Gemma's two larger ones, 63-72% on Gemma's E2B and E4B; on Italian prose Qwen3.5-2B kept about a third of them, and gained next to nothing. One round of 64 tokens is noisy here, a tenth either way between runs. Qwen3-30B-A3B has no such block, nor have the dense Qwen3; the dense Qwen3.5 have one in their original checkpoint, which hf2jns_mtp converts (MODELS.md).

This column was wrong until 26 September 2026, and higher: it measured the block continuing a paragraph that repeated itself, which a model copies and the block guesses almost every time - 107 tok/s for Qwen3.5-2B, 26 for Qwen3.5-9B. The MoE figures of the time (29 and 30) happened to be lower than today's; the ChangeLog has the details.

The comparison with llama.cpp at the top of this page was measured so: llama.cpp (build 2b18470 of 18 September 2026) with its Vulkan backend on the same integrated GPU, everything on it (llama-bench -p 1024 -n 16 -ngl 99 -t 12; the largest model otherwise, below), against janas-bench --prompt 1024 --gen 16 on the same files the same days (9-11 October 2026; llama.cpp's best configuration, Janas-LLM's own choice; on 11 October three rounds each, llama-bench -r 3 and janas-bench --rounds 3, for Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3.5-0.8B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and the models from other hands; Qwen3-Coder-Next as Qwen3-Next-80B, below).

On Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, whose file is larger than this laptop's 30 GB, llama.cpp with its usual build ran out of memory as soon as the GPU took part, even with the experts left on the CPU (-ngl 99 -ncmoe 48): its CPU backend copies the weights into memory of its own to repack them, and the Vulkan backend copies those it leaves to the CPU into buffers the system cannot reclaim. It ran with a build without repacking (GGML_CPU_REPACK=OFF) and two options more, --no-host 1 -lm mmap, which leave the experts in the file, read through the page cache: 16 tok/s reading with the GPU, and 2.8 writing on the CPU alone (with the GPU, 2.0); these are its two figures in the table. Janas-LLM ran the same model with no option of its own, the experts it uses most in a cache of about 19 GB and the rest read from the disk. Janas-LLM's figures are one round each; the writing column is without drafts on both sides. The two tools do not measure in exactly the same way (llama-bench writes without a prompt before it; janas-bench after the 1,024 tokens), and it is one machine. llama.cpp's own CPU backend did worse on this laptop than its Vulkan one at reading (Qwen3-4B 70 tok/s on 20 threads) and as well at writing.

Try it on an idle machine first. The expert cache takes the memory that is free when the model is opened, and what is left of the model is read from disk while it answers, so everything else running takes its share. It degrades gently rather than breaking: measured with a browser and an editor open, the same model kept about three quarters of its speed and waited five times longer on the disk. But the first thing you see should be the machine's real speed, and any measurement you mean to send to others has to be taken with the machine to itself.

Documentation

  • INSTALL.md — what the build needs, how to prepare a model, and the first run

  • docs/serving.md — the model served to MCP clients (janas-mcp) and over HTTP (janas-server)

Getting started

sudo apt install build-essential          # Debian/Ubuntu
sudo apt install libvulkan-dev glslang-tools vulkan-tools   # optional, GPU
sudo pacman -S vulkan-headers glslang vulkan-tools           # the same, Arch

Getting a model

Downloading a model already converted with janas-get, or converting a GGUF file yourself, and which files were checked: docs/models.md.

Using the chat

Filling in code

janas-server fills in code at an editor's cursor, with a model for code such as Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B: OpenAI's /v1/completions with a suffix, and llama.cpp's /infill, which llama.vscode asks. The window sent at every keystroke is kept from moving, so that a keystroke reads only what it changed: 1.5-2.2 s a proposal on a laptop, where a window slid a line was read again in 17 s. How to set it up in VSCodium and VS Code, with llama.vscode or Continue, and what was measured: docs/code-completion.md.

Using it from a program

The library from C and from FreeBASIC and BASIC MODERN, and MCP servers from a program: docs/library.md.

Janas as an MCP server

Using it over HTTP

Measuring your machine

Tools

The converters, checkers and benchmarks built beside the programs: docs/tools.md.

Helping it run on more hardware

Which machines are wanted most, the one command that tries Janas and writes a report, and what to send: docs/hardware.md.

Janas is designed and written by Maurizio "camauri" Cammalleri (LinkedIn, Substack).

It stands on the work of others, and says so:

item.title: AI Is a Tool. Using It Well Takes Skill. (385 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://yyhh.org/blog/2026/10/ai-is-a-tool/, See on Hacker News

In his October 11, 2026 article, "'AI' is Not a Tool," Rich Hickey argues that LLMs are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. I agree that outsourcing work can cost us opportunities to learn. But his conclusion does not follow. Even by his definition, an LLM can be something a human wields. And using it well takes skill, just as using other tools does.

Picking up a saw does not guarantee a straight cut. Holding a chisel does not make you a sculptor. Tools can amplify poor judgment as readily as good judgment. Their usefulness depends on the operator's ability to direct them, interpret feedback, recognize mistakes, and make corrections. Those requirements also apply to LLMs.

An LLM's unpredictability is a meaningful limitation. But predictability, reliability, simplicity, and bounded function are qualities by which we evaluate tools, not prerequisites for membership in the category. A tool does not stop being a tool because it is difficult to control or easy to misuse.

Hickey's distinction between tools and automation also creates a false division. Automation can be a feature of a tool. A compiler performs substantial work without the programmer continuously directing each operation. A spreadsheet recalculates results without someone manually carrying out every calculation. We still wield these systems by specifying inputs, examining results, and deciding what to do next. Why should generating text automatically disqualify an instrument from being a tool when translating code or calculating numbers automatically does not?

The claim that LLM use lacks intention, feedback, direction, and expertise is especially difficult to defend. A programmer can ask an LLM to explain unfamiliar code, challenge that explanation, inspect the source, test a proposed change, reject it, and refine the request. That is a feedback loop directed by a human pursuing a purpose. Doing it well requires knowing what to ask, what evidence matters, and when the answer is wrong. Expertise can make the instrument more useful.

Hickey's concern about reading is valid for a particular use: accepting a summary in place of reading a paper can sacrifice much of what reading teaches. But someone can also read the paper and use an LLM to question their interpretation, explore an objection, or identify something to examine more closely. The possibility of avoiding intellectual work does not establish that every use avoids it. The relevant question is what the person actually does.

What disappoints me the most is the reliance on the AI industry's anthropomorphic vocabulary: "go rogue," "escape containment," "conspire." Repeating those expressions risks accepting the framing that makes these systems sound like independent beings. Software can produce unexpected outputs, fail to follow instructions, or cause harm when given access to consequential actions. Those are real engineering problems. Calling them "conspiracy" adds a suggestion of human motives without establishing any.

I would not claim that an LLM always does exactly what a human tells it to do. It plainly can fail. But failure to obey perfectly does not make it cease to be a tool, any more than successful use proves that its operator has surrendered their judgment.

The useful distinction is between wielding an instrument with skill and delegating work without adequate understanding or oversight. That distinction applies to AI, and it gives us something more practical than declaring that an entire class of software cannot be a tool.

item.title: Who Is Vfmaddrnd231pd? (192 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://purplesyringa.moe/blog/who-is-vfmaddrnd231pd/, See on Hacker News

October 12, 2026

vfmaddrnd231pd is a unique instruction from the FMA instruction set. Most instructions in that set have mnemonics like vfmadd231pd, but here rnd means something very specific. The Intel Software Development Manual documents it as:

VFMADDRND231PD – Fused Multiply-Add of Packed Double-Precision Floating-Point Values with rounding control

[…] The immediate byte defines several bit fields that control rounding, DAZ, FTZ, and exception suppression (See Table 5-3).

Most x86 floating-point instructions use the global rounding mode and settings, changing which is pretty slow. But vfmaddrnd231pd allows the rounding mode to be controlled on a per-instruction basis, and since FMA can emulate addition, subtraction, and multiplication, this mechanism effectively allows any arithmetic to have controllable rounding without AVX-512 – making some algorithms that rely on rounding incredibly faster.

Or so it would, if this instruction actually existed. GNU assembler doesn’t recognize it. The Intel C/C++ Compiler intrinsics _mm_fmaddround_pd and _mm256_fmaddround_pd that SDM mentions are absent not only from Clang, but from ICC as well. Trying to assemble the instructions by hand from the SDM opcode list reveals another issue:

VEX.DDS.128.66.0F3A.W1 B8 /r /ib

VEX is the VEX prefix, but what is DDS? This opcode is the only mention of DDS in the SDM, and this SO answer says that DDS is merely used for documentation and was removed from later SDM versions, but the fact that it’s still present here is suspicious. And when you actually run the instruction on a CPU that supports the FMA instruction set, like my Haswell, it raises #UD (“UnDefined instruction”)!

I already found it strange that the SDM only lists vfmaddrnd231pd and not other variants like using pd/ps/sd/ss or 132/213/231, which other FMA instructions have, but this confirmed my suspicions. It was at that point that I downloaded a more recent version of the SDM and noticed that this instruction is absent in the 2026 edition of the SDM, despite being present in the 2024 version.

I must say I’m incredibly confused. This instruction doesn’t look like a typo in the documentation, since the docs contain unique tables and pseudocode that isn’t similar to any other instruction. My best hypothesis is that Intel wanted to add the vfmaddrnd* set, then found an issue with it at the last moment and removed it from the CPU, but didn’t quite adjust the SDM correctly. But I have no way to confirm that.

If anyone reading this has a friend at Intel, I’d love to know the answer.

item.title: Writing a Demoscene Intro for the ZX Spectrum (119 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.markround.com/blog/2026/zx-spectrum-intro, See on Hacker News

A look at the tools, techniques and challenges of creating a retro-style 'crack intro'

Updated: October 12, 2026

Download Now View on pouet.net Discussion on Hacker News

Intro

In the late 80s, I spent an embarrassing number of hours hunched over my ZX Spectrum, typing in Sinclair BASIC programs and rudimentary assembler routines copied from magazines, trying to re-create the Amiga crack intros I’d seen round at a friend’s house. Obviously, they never came even slightly close - but now, many decades later, I’ve finally managed it! I’m now the proud author of a hand-rolled retro demoscene intro that runs on a stock 128Kb Spectrum. It features all those late 80s tropes: A smooth scrolltext (with ‘leet custom fonts!), a three-channel AY soundtrack, bouncing VU meters and the essential parallax starfield. It’s currently 10287 bytes of code, or 19552 bytes as a complete tape image - which, given I’ve been working on this since December 13th last year, means my average rate of code-production is a paltry ~ 455 bytes per week!

This blog post is a technical overview of how I got there, some cool tricks I picked up, and everything I had to learn (and re-learn) about the Speccy and Z80 assembly along the way. It simultaneously rates as one of my favourite side-projects ever, and also the one that most often nearly triggered a foot put through my monitor in frustration. I’ll reflect on all that at the end, but for now if you just want to see the finished product, the download button is at the top of the article and the included .tap cassette tape image should load into any emulator. There’s also a YouTube capture, links to the production on pouet.net, and you can run it from within a web browser by visiting my TNFS site portal - check option 4 for recent uploads.

Be Kind, Rewind

But let’s skip back briefly to the late 80s. Coming from the world of an 8-bit, cassette tape loading computer, seeing an Amiga for the first time was like encountering something from outer space. Like everyone who saw one back in the day, I was blown away by the amazing graphics and sound on display, not to mention the library of ground-breaking games. But I found myself even more captivated by the mysterious (and totally badass) “intros” displayed at the beginning of pirated games.

Created by the software piracy groups that had cracked the copy protection and distributed the floppy-disk based games, they were mini works of art in their own right - music, graphics and usually some cool-looking effect to show off the group’s prowess. There’s a great collection of these intros (or “cracktros”) archived on YouTube.

Watch a few of those videos and you’ll quickly notice the “design” tropes that almost every cracktro shares: a cool, edgy logo at the top of the screen (bonus points if it’s dripping blood or in any way “metal”), some boastful text displayed on top of an effect of some sort - usually a scrolling parallax starfield, or rotating 3d object - and a further scroll-text full of shout outs, greetings to fellow pseudonymous crackers and adverts for illegal BBS systems galore. Needless to say, to a kid in the 80s/early 90s this was possibly the coolest thing ever.

I thought this one was the absolute bomb when I first saw it. Sine-scroller, pirate BBS adverts, cool logo with a sword - and of course, a starfield. There’s something for everyone here.

The music from this is burned into my brain. I think pretty much everyone of my classmates knew this intro given the popularity of Lemmings in the early 90s. Skid Row as a group are still active to this day and this is probably the quintessential Amiga cracktro of the period.

Endless Piracy. Edgy. Another cool logo, sine-wave scroller, starfield and boasting text. The classics never go out of style.

Another great combination of all the essential ingredients. Cool logo, even cooler text font, scrolling starfield and a scroll-text running along the bottom. Vintage stuff.

Logo. Text. Scroller. But no starfield - otherwise a solid effort from Anthrox here :)

The demoscene grew out of these intros. The cracking eventually faded into the background, and coders, “graphicians” and musicians all contributed to feature-length productions that showcased their abilities, competed with other groups and pushed the machine to its limits. In amazing feats of ingenuity and pure “code as an art form”, the scene lives on today, with groups producing breathtaking productions like this and this - bear in mind, both of those are running on a 7Mhz home computer equipped with a floppy disk, 1Mb of memory and a sound chip from 1985.

But much as I admire the sheer skill and dedication that takes, it’s the early “single screen” scrolly-text-and-starfield cracktros I’ve always found captivating. They took on a sort of mystical quality for me, hinting at a scene and a culture I could only ever experience from the outside - which is exactly why I spent all those hours in Sinclair BASIC, trying in vain to re-create them, and dreaming of the day I’d eventually have an Amiga of my own.

The Jump Back

I eventually did trade up to a range of Amiga systems, joined a few “scene” groups myself and threw myself into a variety of activities until exams and the end of my teenage years beckoned. I dabbled with Z80 code back then, and at one point knew enough 68k assembly to bluff my way through - partly from the Amiga’s heyday, partly from a few “embedded systems” modules at University where I had to program a set of traffic lights or lift-controllers. Given there’s not much call for that sort of thing at my $DAYJOB, though, it had all pretty much faded from my memory.

I have kept working on a bunch of projects in my spare time, and one of my favourites is my TNFS site - sort of an old-school BBS system or interactive “website” for the Spectrum, which grew out of a fun experiment to see how far I could push Sinclair BASIC. It relies on a modern network card fitted to the Spectrum, which is how I came to be chatting to “Desertkun”, another TNFS-protocol enthusiast. He’s now producing a great new WiFi network card for the Speccy, and was kind enough to send me a few of the prototypes to test out for him.

I was massively inspired by his hardware and low-level coding chops, and during one of our video calls where we’d been comparing our development setups, he asked why I didn’t write any Z80 assembly myself. A throw-away comment, but the challenge was set! Now, I couldn’t face re-writing the whole site in asm, but I figured I could produce a self-contained intro to promote it in the style of the early “BBStros”, and finally be one of the cool kids with a scene production of my own :)

I mean, how hard could it be ? (ooooh - foreshadowing!)

Dev Environment

My development environment through this was pretty straightforward, and is the same stack I use for developing my TNFS site. I just used a Makefile-driven build system which ran my code through the Pasmo assembler, my fork of zmakebas to build BASIC files, and the FUSE emulator for testing. For final testing on the real hardware, I uploaded my .tap files to my local TNFS server where I could run them on my +3.

A few additional tools I have to call out because they ended up making a big difference - one is the amazing web-based “asm-editor” I discovered while looking up Z80 instructions. Not only does this site have a great reference of all the Z80 instructions, but it also has an editor where you can run example code and see how the memory and/or various registers change state. Take for example, the djnz instruction - you can build it and step through the example loop construct one instruction at a time. Or try my example of an add instruction in the screenshot to see how the carry flag works when a bit gets shifted out of a register. Although it uses a slightly different syntax to Pasmo (so I couldn’t drop my code directly in it), it massively helped when manually stepping through things.

And lastly, probably the most significant debugging tools I used on this project - a notepad and pen, and my two dogs (say “Hi!” to Biscuit & Pebble…) I’ll write some more about this in the wrap-up, but this really was a highly unusual project for me, coming from decades of much higher-level languages and constructs. Most of my z80 code I only ever really understood after drawing out the bytes and bitmasks, keeping a table of register flags and drawing chunks of screen memory out by hand. And I found my evening walks with the two dogs provided ideal rubber duck exercises, although I’m not sure what they both made of my protracted mutterings about the hl register pair. Either way, debugging-by-dog is highly recommended!

The Starting Point

So, let’s get started. I followed a great “Hello, world!” example from futurice.com to validate my build environment. Beyond that, the first thing I wanted to do was load in my logo and background image I’d use as a “stage” for the remainder of the planned intro. I wasn’t really sure what I was going to do at this point, just that I wanted my logo at the top, and a scrolltext along the bottom row of the screen. As my TNFS site header already looked kinda demoscene-y, I made a quick edit putting in place two blue guide-bars inside which I’d put further content.

A Spectrum SCREEN$ file (usually displayed as loading screens) is just a dump of screen memory, starting from byte 16384, and running for 6912 bytes. The weird layout of this is very relevant later, but in order to display it all you need to do is load your file into that memory location. After a few hour’s work of reviewing Speccy internals and following various guides, I had a very simple starting point for my demo that served as the basis for everything else that came after.

org $8000

screen  EQU $4000 ; address of the first byte of screen memory, 16384 in dec
scrlen  EQU 6912  ; total length of the screen memory inc. attributes
ula     EQU $FE   ; I/O port for the ULA to control the border
black   EQU 0     ; Spectrum colour number, the exact same ones BASIC uses

start:
  ld a,black      ; Set the border colour to black using the ULA
  out (ula),a

  ; Copy my logo header picture to screen memory
  ld hl,header    ; HL = location of my screen file in this code
  ld de,screen    ; DE = start of screen memory
  ld bc,scrlen    ; BC = 6912 bytes to copy
  ldir            ; block copy, see https://jnz.dk/z80/ldir.html

; busy loop - rest of intro goes here :P                    
hold:
  halt            ; sleep until the next interrupt (1/50 second)
  jr hold         ; then jump back and sleep again, for ever

header:
  incbin "assets/header.scr"  ; my logo header/background

end start

Not much to look at now, but this simple starting point introduced me to important concepts like interfacing with the Spectrum’s hardware (ULA chip to start with, and AY sound chip later) via the out instruction, how to pull in binary files using Pasmo’s INCBIN directive, using the Z80’s block copy ldir instruction, the use of register pairs for 16-bit addressing, and simple branching to labels.

Hello World

The next step was to print something on the screen and explore some of the Speccy’s built-in ROM routines, which are somewhat analagous to syscalls on modern operating systems. There are plenty of disassemblies and guides to the Spectrum ROM available on the internet, one of the best commented and linked one is at https://skoolkid.github.io/rom/. Using this as a reference alongside the various “Hello, world!” tutorials showed me how this sort of thing is built up:

  at      EQU 22 ; "at" control character used to position the cursor
  row     EQU 11 ; coordinates where to print the message
  col     EQU 9

  prstring EQU $203C ; where the pr_string routine lives in ROM

  ld de,msg        ; DE = address of the first character
  ld bc,msglen     ; BC = how many characters to print
  call prstring    ; print the lot

; busy loop is the same...

msg:
  db at,row,col            ; equivalent of "PRINT AT 11,9" in BASIC
  db "Hello, world!"
msglen  EQU $-msg          ; 16 bytes in all, pasmo shortcut, $=program counter

I ended up mostly not using the ROM routines in my code as they dragged in all sorts of things I didn’t need, but it was massively useful to understand how they worked as they introduced me to yet more commonly-used constructs. For example, the PR_STRING routine defined here shows how you can build a loop over each character. If you’re just starting out, I highly recommend going over the 8 lines in that routine with a notepad and pen, working out the contents of the registers and following the loop constructs.

I also made a version of it in asm-editor you can try. If you click that link, you’ll see a version of the code loaded into the web editor. Click “Build”, and then step through the code using the “Step” button - although no text will be actually displayed (I skipped over the call to the Spectrum ROM “restart” vector that does this), you’ll see the various states of the registers and for example the BC register counting down as each byte of the string is processed.

; Picking our own font is simply a matter of over-writing this

  ld hl,myfont-256 ; HL = font address - 256 as per docs

Strap in folks, we’re leaving lamer city… So at this point, a month or so in to my dabblings and I’d started to get a reasonable understanding of common idioms and was starting to feel like this was a project that might actually go somewhere. The problem started when I moved on to trying to implement actual demo effects: It became very apparent, very quickly, just how much I didn’t know about how this all worked. Cursed Screen Layout

The first such problem - and the cause of probably 90% of my pain - is the Speccy’s extremely weird screen layout. Rather than standard bitmapped display you might expect on more modern hardware, it is instead split into 3 sections, each with a set of interleaved rows (so if you keep adding 1 to a screen address, eventually instead of reaching the next row, you’ll instead end up 8 rows down, and so on until you hit the bottom of the section and then loop back to the row underneath where you started!) followed by a block of “attribute” bytes which determine the colours of each 8x8 block. The attribute blocks are the reason why each 8x8 character cell can only have two colours (a PAPER and INK attribute) which led to the garish “colour-clash” of spectrum games and distinctive style where artists try to keep inside 8x8 blocks as much as possible. But it was the layout of the bitmap portion that is such a mind twister.

You can see this illustrated whenever a game reads in a loading screen from tape. You can see each section built up with the interleaved rows one at a time, and then finally the colour and other attributes (like flashing ). There’s a lot of detail at the fantastic Break Into Program site. In the defense of the designers, they were working with extremely limited hardware and I don’t think the Speccy was ever imagined as a games machine. When you start shuffling bytes around, you realise that this approach is really optimised for displaying text which is neatly arranged into 8x8 character boundaries. For example, using this “scrambled” bit order, if you have a screen address in the hl register pair, you can quickly get to the next pixel line of a given address by simply incrementing the “high” byte. There’s a bunch of other “cheap moves” you can make by simply shifting bits around:

Move Instruction
Right 8 pixels inc l
Left 8 pixels dec l
Down 1 pixel line inc h
Up 1 pixel line dec h
Down 1 character row add 32 to l

It was a reasonable choice for a machine that would probably spend a lot of it’s time displaying BASIC program listings - it’s only when you start trying to write demo or sprite routines that it starts to feel really weird. This also means you’ll pretty quickly need a routine to convert X,Y addresses to the relevant memory addresses. Again, L Break Into Program has a useful routine and if you disassemble more or less any spectrum game or demo, you’ll find a version of this procedure somewhere. And yes, this all became horribly relevant later on…

Admittedly, not the most interesting demonstration - but this was the first time I had made something move on the Spectrum’s screen with assembly! I watched this with pride more times than I care to admit :)

I had a snazzy logo and “Hello World” text, but that doesn’t make for a very interesting intro! The first effect I wanted was the scrolltext - without that, it’s not really an intro. Now, the Amiga had all kinds of hardware sprites, blitter operations, custom chips but the Spectrum had none of that. I was going to have to work out how to do things the hard way - “banging on the metal”, literally by shifting bits around the screen memory by hand and having the CPU do all the work.

This is where understanding the Speccy’s weird screen and character cell layout is so important. It turns out there’s a neat trick as long as I stay inside one character row - there’s a RL instruction, which takes a byte and “rotates” it left. It inserts whatever is in the carry flag into the rightmost bit, and whatever gets shifted out ends up in the carry bit again. That means if you string a bunch of them together, you can move a set of pixels across the screen - the moment they “fall off” one character cell, they end up in the carry flag and then the next rl instruction inserts them at the beginning of the next character cell to the left. Repeat 32 times, and you’ve just moved a pixel (or set of pixels) across a line of the screen:

linestart EQU $4880         ; leftmost byte of the line 12 rows down
lineend   EQU linestart+31  ; rightmost byte column ($489F) 
linelen   EQU 32            ; one whole line is 32 bytes (character cells) across
dot       EQU %00000001     ; the dot "shape", just one pixel lit at the far right end

newdot:
  ld a,dot                 ; load the dot shape (only rightmost pixel lit) into a
  ld (lineend),a           ; store it in the rightmost byte of the line, pixel is now lit

frame:
  halt                     ; wait for the next frame, otherwise it whizzes across too fast to see
  ld hl,lineend            ; hl = last (rightmost) byte of the line
  ld b,linelen             ; loop counter, 32 bytes to work through
  or a                     ; trick to clear the carry flag, or against itself leaves a register 
                           ; unchanged but clears various bits including the carry flag
                           ; see https://jnz.dk/z80/or_r.html
shift:
  rl (hl)                  ; rotate this byte left (00000001 -> 00000010)
  dec hl                   ; point hl at the next byte to the left
  djnz shift               ; loop construct: b=b-1 and then jump back to shift label until b=0
  jr c,newdot              ; now we've shifted the whole line, so if the carry flag is set now it means
                           ; the dot has just left the screen, so we jump back to the start
  jr frame                 ; otherwise it is still somewhere on the screen, so keep shifting!

Wrapping this in another loop that increments h each time (remember - that gets us moving down a scanline) gets us moving an entire character cell. Here you can see it moving an entire row of my “Hello world” message. There was however a lot more work needed to make a proper scrolltext, with each letter appearing smoothly. I started off by just printing an entire character at a time on the right-hand edge of the screen - it worked, but was pretty ugly as you saw each new character appear at once in the right-hand side of the screen, scrolling 8 pixels over and then the next character flashed up. Instead, I wanted to make each character appear pixel by pixel and that required a bit more bit juggling. The routine I ended up with effectively streams each character in, line by line, pixel by pixel using the font data directly instead of calling the ROM print character routine.

It does this by looking up the ASCII code for a character, and then fetching the corresponding font representation into a 8-byte buffer, one byte for each line of data. The font data starts with the space character (character code 32), so a lookup is simply font code base address + (ascii code - 32) * 8 to get to the bits for that letter.

Arranged into an 8x8 grid, the bits for the letter H in the font data look like this. For each row of bits, I shift the line left using a neat trick. The byte is loaded into the a register, and then by adding itself to itself - add a,a we shift the value left (in binary, multiplying by 2 moves everything over one bit) so that the pixel I want to draw ends up dropping into the carry flag. This is an idiomatic way of doing it in Z80 code as it’s faster and smaller than the sla instruction. And every cycle quickly adds up when you’re re-drawing 256 bytes every frame!

The character buffer then looks like this, with the top line shifted. Now, with the hl register pair pointing at the correct location on the screen, I can then use the rl trick discussed above. This shifts a scanline from the bottom character row of the screen left by one pixel and draws my pixel in the rightmost position by moving it in from the carry flag. Looping 32 times over this moves the entire row by 1 pixel with my new pixel inserted at the right.

I then repeat this step again using inc h to move down one scan line until the entire character column has been drawn. At this point, the character buffer looks like this, and all 8 lines of the bottom screen row have all been shifted left by one bit by looping over all 32 character columns. The whole thing then repeats another 7 times until the entire character has been smoothly scrolled onto the screen.

So just to re-state this because I think it’s worth the emphasis - just to scroll a message across the bottom of the screen, we’re having to loop over and re-draw 256 pixels every frame! It shows how much faster assembly is than the BASIC interpreter built into the spectrum’s ROM. I found it amazing to see my code finally working and imagining all the bits flying around and registers flapping away. It really makes me appreciate just how much effort went into creating the games I played back then.

Music

The original Amiga module I converted. A proper 1980s ear-worm!

Of course, any good intro needs some music. On the Amiga, the standard was the “tracker” module format, which has a long and involved history of different forks, versions and tweaks. A song is built up from a series of patterns, each made up of rows of instructions. Each instruction usually includes note or pitch information, which sample to play and various parameters such as volume, effects - or in the case of some instructions, which position in the song to jump to. In many ways, it’s almost like a programming language for music. Using ProTracker as an example, a typical note cell is 4 bytes, shown on-screen as something like C-2 01 C20. That breaks down into three fields: the note and octave (C-2), the sample number (01), and the effect and its parameter (C20 - in this case, “set the volume to $20”, which is half of the maximum $40).

A close-up of Protracker playing a tune. Note the VUmeters - another classic demo effect I would pinch later on!

For an impressive demonstration of what’s possible with a tracker and to see what the note data looks like on-screen, check out the work of h0ffman, and in particular his winning “Professional Tracker” entry from the Revision 2014 competition. He’s an undisputed master of the science (or art!) of tracking, and his “Secrets of Protracker” talk gives a great overview of what’s possible.

The Amiga’s sound hardware far eclipsed anything else on the market at the time, and the ZX Spectrum is paltry by comparison. The original 48K models only offered a rudimentary “beeper”, but the later 128K models included a 3-channel AY-3-8912 sound chip. This was very popular in 8-bit micros of the time, and a more-or-less identical variant was also used in the Atari ST. While it only offers basic waveforms and sound processing, it does enable multi-channel “chip music”, and so it became the mainstay of the ZX Spectrum demoscene. It also spawned a variety of SoundTracker clones on the Spectrum itself, although most musicians these days prefer to work in modern tools like Vortex Tracker II, which runs natively under Windows.

The Conversion

Pex looking back on his demos - this starts at the point where he features my letter and plays a bit of my cover version!

For my intro, I wanted to port an Amiga module - and I had the perfect one in mind. One of my favourite Amiga music disks was “Sounds Of Gnome”, released in 1989 by the Swedish duo “Mahoney & Kaktus”. Mahoney also wrote NoiseTracker, one of the first really widely used trackers on the Amiga, and the program that served as my teenage introduction to making computer music of my own. Back in 2018 I made a rock cover of one of the other tunes on that disk, and wrote to Mahoney (real name “Pex”) about it. He ended up showing my “music video” at a demo conference, which I am eternally grateful for! So it seemed only fitting that I mangle another song from that collection with a Spectrum conversion… Sorry, guys! I picked the track “Milkman” which was written by “Glue Master”, an associate of Mahoney’s who had a few of his tracks featured on the compilation.

It’s an ideal track for converting: It’s short (only 7 patterns in total), most of those patterns share the same chord sequence, and it looked fairly easy to squeeze the original 4 channels down into the Spectrum’s 3. Plus, it’s an incredibly catchy tune and I knew it well - I’ve been listening to it for 35+ years and often jam along to it on guitar or bass. The conversion started off pretty easily: all I really had to do was copy the patterns note-for-note from the Amiga mod, which I had open in OpenMPT as my Windows tracker. Below is a session with both trackers open on the same pattern - the original Amiga mod on the left, and my 3-channel Spectrum conversion on the right.

Note the 11.7 in the 3rd channel of the Spectrum version. This is a “pitch slide down” effect in Vortex Tracker syntax, which drops the pitch by about a quarter-tone. It’s repeated on the next line, so the overall effect is a slide down from the A# that leads in to the next bass note. The original Amiga mod does the same thing using its own syntax - those are the 202s you can see on the same notes, at the bottom of the 4th track.

Using just a single “beep” sound for everything was enough to check everything was working, and after a few weeks of hacking on it and re-arranging things in the evenings, I had a basic version which sounded surprisingly good for a first draft:

I have to give a special mention to this forum post which was a massive help getting me started. It’s probably the best introduction to Vortex Tracker I’ve found - many, many thanks to the original author for taking the time to write it all up!

The real challenge was making it sound as close to the original as possible. That meant building up a library of better-sounding samples for the different parts, and making extensive use of Vortex Tracker’s “ornaments”. Vortex Tracker comes with a great selection of sounds, and fortunately I’m also a weirdo who likes to listen to chiptunes in the background while I work! So whenever I found something particularly enticing, I filed it away for later pilfering inspiration. A Vortex Tracker sample isn’t really a “sample” in the Amiga sense of a recorded sound - it’s a definition of how a note sounds, one line per frame. Each line can mix in a tone or the white noise generator (useful for snare effects and suchlike), along with various other parameters.

Ornaments, on the other hand, give you extra control over what pitch a note plays - and this enables really useful tricks like “arpeggio chords”. For example, an ornament of 0,4 makes the channel switch rapidly (25 times a second) between the note being played and the one 4 semitones above it. It happens so quickly that it sounds much like two notes played at the same time, which means you can build up full-sounding triad chords using only two channels. Take the opening chord in my fully converted version, Cm: It plays C in the first channel and the minor 3rd (D#) in the second, then I apply an ornament to the second channel to bring it up 4 semitones to the 5th (G). That gives all three notes of the chord, while keeping the 3rd channel free for other parts.

As well as making much more efficient use of the limited 3 channels, this also gives Spectrum music that characteristic “warbling” sound, which I find really appealing in a retro kind of way! Between tricks like this and samples that mix tones with white noise (to make a combined “bass-snare” sound, for example), I managed to condense the full track down to 3 channels. Many months later, I have to say I’m really pleased with the final result.

Playback

The original site that was home to Vortex Tracker, documentation and other resources appears to be offline at the moment. I managed to grab a copy of everything I needed from archive.org - you’ll want the PTxTools.7z file for the playback routines discussed here.

Update - a user on Hacker News added this useful bit of information: “Sergey Bulba’s WWW site is still around and the relevant stuff can be found today at https://ay.strangled.net/progr_e.htm”. Thanks, JdeBP!

The playback was simple in theory: As this overview notes, you basically just pull in the player routine, include your module file and call the playback routine once per frame in your main loop. The catch is, none of the source code versions supplied in the archive worked with my Pasmo assembler. Fortunately, there is a pre-compiled binary object shipped alongside the source (VTII10bG in the PTxTools/PT3Play directory). This just has to be loaded in at address $C000 - this cannot be changed, as it has lots of absolute addresses baked in.

My code to handle module playback now looks something like this, with the binary module loaded in place:

; Define the start address of the player routine and functions we need
player EQU $C000      ; hard-coded org address of binary player
plinit EQU player+3   ; init function in docs, module address in hl
plplay EQU player+5   ; play and move on one frame

; from the docs - this "analyzes PT3 module header and prepares 
; corresponding note and volume tables"
ld hl,moduleimg
call plinit

; main loop
hold:
  halt
  call plplay
  call scroll
  ; other effects / routines go here...
  jr hold

moduleimg:
  incbin "assets/music.pt3"

Starfield

This brings me to the main event. No self-respecting cracktro is complete without a starfield!

My first, naive approach to the classic starfield effect was to scatter random stars across the screen, then move down each scan-line applying the same rl trick I’d used for the scroll-text. I figured I could get parallax by shifting each row a different amount: One pixel for the first row, two for the second, three for the third, then back to one again, all the way down the screen to give the impression of several “fields” of stars moving at different speeds.

It turned out there were two major problems with that approach. Firstly, shifting an entire row smeared whatever else was on it along with the stars - which I’d expected, and had filed away as a problem for future me. The bigger issue was speed: by the time I’d finished the first three rows I’d already performed hundreds of shift operations, and it was nowhere near fast enough to fit inside a single frame. Everything crawled across the screen, and the music playback slowed down so much that you could actually hear the arpeggio ornaments warbling away as separate notes.

Clearly I was going to have to keep track of the individual stars instead. I found this routine, which was more-or-less what I had in mind and started me off with the idea of a structure to hold the state of each star. It also uses a screen address lookup much like the one from “Break Into Program”.

That got things moving, but the co-ordinate lookup and tracking proved expensive to do (it has to run for every star, every frame as well as keep track of the old position for erasing) and I’d been ignoring the bigger question how to display stuff on top of the starfield. My original idea was simply to draw the stars and then paint text over them each frame, which blew the frame budget just as comprehensively as my first attempt.

If I wanted something more interesting than an empty starfield, I’d have to keep track of which cells were occupied by text and avoid drawing stars in them in the first place, rather than over-painting them every time. After lots of scribbling in my notepad and visualising rows of bits, I eventually solved both challenges by “cheating” fairly liberally.

So now, I don’t generate a random starfield at all. Instead, I built a table of pre-calculated Y and X position pairs:

stdata:
  defb 109, 25,  88,182,  42, 96, 155,226
  defb  59,254, 137,169, 160, 84, 125,193
  ; ... and so on, for 32 stars ...

This saves faffing about with an RNG, and once I have a layout that looks good I know it’ll always look good. I can also “fudge” things and ensure no two stars share the same y co-ordinate which sidesteps a whole class of problems like stars sharing a scanline, and having to deal with them overtaking each other.

The “random” layout is generated by a simple Ruby script:

#!/usr/bin/env ruby

PAIRS    = 32
PER_LINE = 4          # pairs per line
Y_RANGE  = 40..175    # exclude rows taken up by my logo & bars
X_RANGE  = 0..255

raise "y range too small" if Y_RANGE.size < PAIRS

# no duplicate y values
ys    = Y_RANGE.to_a.sample(PAIRS)
pairs = ys.map { |y| [y, rand(X_RANGE)] }

pairs.each_slice(PER_LINE) do |row|
  body = row.map { |y, x| format('%3d,%3d,', y, x) }.join(' ')
  puts "defb #{body.chomp(',')}"
end

When the routine initialises, I convert those co-ordinate pairs into a table that tracks the state of each star. So rather than storing a position and translating it to a screen address every frame, each of my star records now looks like this (offsets from the base address):

STSCR   EQU 0  ; screen address of the byte the star is in, e.g. $4123 
STOCC   EQU 2  ; a pointer to the "occupancy check" table cell
STMASK  EQU 4  ; the star's bit pattern, e.g. %00010000 
STSTEP  EQU 5  ; "speed" - num. of pixels this star travels per frame

The key thing is that there are no X/Y co-ordinates at all. For each star I store the screen byte it sits in and the bit mask within that byte, so it’s already in the form the screen writes need. That means no address conversion per frame, just simple bit shifting and rotation.

Moving a star is then dead simple. I rotate its mask left with rlca, and when the bit rotates out of bit 7, it lands back in bit 0 with the carry flag set. That’s the signal I need to move the star one character cell to the left, which is one of the “cheap moves” from earlier.

Because I’m tracking which cell each star is in, the collision check comes almost for free. That’s what the second pointer is for: STOCC (Star Occupancy) moves in step with STSCR through a table holding one byte per character cell. The “typewriter” routine sets a byte to 1 for every cell containing a text character or the cursor, so checking whether a star is hidden behind text is a single or instruction. If the cell is occupied, I skip drawing the star but carry on rotating and stepping it along until it reaches a cell where it can be displayed:

ld l,(ix+STOCC)
ld h,(ix+STOCC+1)
ld a,(hl)                ; A = the occupancy check for this cell
or a                     ; test A against zero
jr nz,stmove             ; it's occupied, so leave the screen alone

Parallax is still handled by moving each star a different number of pixels per frame, but the cost is a lot lower this time as I’m only touching the cells the stars actually occupy, rather than every byte of every row.

That’s looking more like it! The typewriter routine is a simple copy of the font data from memory, and is very cheap as we can use the “cheap moves” to quickly fetch the 8x8 block.

I also skip drawing any space character so it leaves the “occupancy cell” unmarked. This means the stars keep drifting through the gaps in the text - you can see here the odd star passing in between the words. I switched to ALL CAPS writing for the final version which helps the effect even more as the font is quite blocky, so you don’t really notice stars skipping the spaces inside a glyph at all.
